```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The estimator of the case, for spec_frame()
source("../R/housing/_tools.R")

audit <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
subgroups <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/display_subgroups.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about estimating an effect separately in parts of a sample, and about what follows from making many such estimates at once. The housing-audit case comes from a field experiment by the original authors (OAs), who emailed public housing authorities across the United States from names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]; the [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd) tells it in full. The claim of the course concerns all the names together: replies to Hispanic names opened with the name of the sender less often than replies to white names. The paper also asked narrower questions of the same data, whether officials treat applicants of their own group differently and whether the gap depends on the composition of the community, and its abstract reports that the disparity in tone "is somewhat more muted in more diverse locations, but it does not depend on whether a housing official is Hispanic". Questions of this kind divide the replies into subgroups, and each division adds comparisons, each with its own chance of a false alarm. Every number on the page is computed when it is built, from the files of the case in `cases/housing/data/`.

## 1. The subgroups of the case {#sec-subgroups}

The pipeline stage `R/housing/05_displays.R` writes `display_subgroups.csv`, which holds the gap of the claim in seven subgroups beside the gap among all the coded replies. Each row is the same comparison as the reference specification of the course, the difference in the share of named greetings between replies to Hispanic and to white names, with HC2 standard errors, fitted to a subset of the replies, and the [codebook of the displays](../cases/housing/data/displays_codebook.md) documents the columns. The seven subgroups come from three divisions of the replies, which differ in what they can tell us.

- **The sex of the name.** Santiago against Brett and Gabriela against Emily. The sex of the name was crossed with the group by design, so each half is an experiment of its own, randomised like the whole.
- **The official who replied.** Replies from officials with distinctively Hispanic names and from all other officials, the test of the second hypothesis of the paper. An official is known only by replying, so this division is selected after the email arrived, and the [module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) sets out why such a comparison needs more care.
- **The community.** The lower, middle and top third of communities by percent Hispanic, the question of the third hypothesis, which the paper tested with separate models for each group of names (pp. 20–22). The thirds come from the 2012 estimates of the American Community Survey, made before the emails went out, and they lack `r sum(is.na(ref$hispanic_third))` of the `r nrow(ref)` replies, as the [missing-values module](missingness.qmd#sec-covariates) explains.

```{r}
#| label: fig-subgroups
#| fig-cap: "The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the coded replies, overall and in seven subgroups, with 95% confidence intervals from HC2 standard errors; the number of replies in each comparison is printed on the right. Source: `cases/housing/data/display_subgroups.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of eight gaps with intervals. All lie below zero, between about −26 and −15 points; the interval for officials with Hispanic names runs from about −64 to +13, and those for the female names and for the middle third of communities reach or cross zero."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| code-fold: true
subgroups |>
  datawizard::data_modify(subgroup = factor(subgroup, levels = rev(subgroup)),
                          label = paste(n, "replies")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = b_pp, y = subgroup)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#9aa8b3") +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), size = 0.35, linewidth = 0.7,
                           colour = "#1d2733") +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(x = 22, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "#5b6770") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-65, 35)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap in greetings by name, Hispanic minus white names (points)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-values
#| include: false
officials <- datawizard::data_filter(subgroups, subgroup == "replies from officials with Hispanic names")
```

All eight gaps lie in the direction of the claim, from `r insight::format_value(max(subgroups$b_pp), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(min(subgroups$b_pp), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, and `r sum(subgroups$p[subgroups$subgroup != "all names"] < 0.05)` of the seven subgroup gaps are significant at the 5% level when each is tested on its own. The intervals differ more than the estimates do, because the subgroups differ in size: the gap among the `r officials$n` replies from officials with Hispanic names, `r insight::format_value(officials$b_pp, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, is the largest of all and the least certain, with an interval from `r insight::format_value(officials$ci_low, digits = 0, style_negative = "minus")` to +`r insight::format_value(officials$ci_high, digits = 0)` points.

## 2. Why the number of comparisons matters {#sec-multiplicity}

A test at the 5% level rejects a true null hypothesis once in twenty times, by construction. A study that runs seven such tests on effects that are all zero, and reports whichever of them comes out significant, runs a much larger risk of reporting something false. If the seven tests were independent, the chance that at least one of them would reject is $1 - 0.95^7$, or `r insight::format_value(100 * (1 - 0.95^7), digits = 0)`%. The tests of this case are not independent, since the divisions overlap and every reply sits in three of the subgroups, but the arithmetic shows the direction of the problem: the more comparisons a study makes, the more of its significant results chance alone will supply.

The subgroups of a study raise a second problem, which is often the more serious one. The question of interest is usually whether the gap differs between subgroups, and that question is not answered by finding the gap significant in one subgroup and not in another. @GelmanStern2006DifferenceSignificantNot made the point in their title, "The Difference Between 'Significant' and 'Not Significant' is not Itself Statistically Significant", and in their first paragraph: "even large changes in significance levels can correspond to small, nonsignificant changes in the underlying quantities" (p. 328). On this case, the gap is significant for the male names and only just for the female names, significant in the lower and top thirds of communities and not in the middle third, and significant among the replies from other officials but not among those from officials with Hispanic names. Each pair invites a story. The tests of the differences themselves, which ask whether the gap changes from one subgroup to the next, give none.

```{r}
#| label: differences
# The difference between the gaps for male and female names, and between
# officials with and without Hispanic names: the interaction of a linear
# probability model, with HC2 errors
by_sex <- stats::lm(y ~ hisp * name_sex, data = ref) |>
  parameters::model_parameters(vcov = "HC2") |>
  datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp:name_sexmale")
by_official <- stats::lm(y ~ hisp * hispanic_official, data = ref) |>
  parameters::model_parameters(vcov = "HC2") |>
  datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp:hispanic_official")
# The three thirds are separate sets of replies, so the test that their gaps
# are equal is the test of heterogeneity of a meta-analysis (metafor)
thirds <- datawizard::data_filter(subgroups, startsWith(subgroup, "communities"))
by_third <- metafor::rma(yi = b_pp, sei = se_pp, data = thirds, method = "EE")
round(c(sex_diff_pp = 100 * by_sex$Coefficient, sex_p = by_sex$p,
        official_diff_pp = 100 * by_official$Coefficient, official_p = by_official$p,
        thirds_Q = by_third$QE, thirds_p = by_third$QEp), 3)
```

The gap for the male names is `r insight::format_value(abs(100 * by_sex$Coefficient), digits = 1)` points wider than for the female names (`r insight::format_p(by_sex$p, stars = FALSE)`), the gap in replies from officials with Hispanic names is `r insight::format_value(abs(100 * by_official$Coefficient), digits = 1)` points wider than in replies from other officials (`r insight::format_p(by_official$p, stars = FALSE)`), and the three thirds of communities differ by no more than chance would produce (Q = `r insight::format_value(by_third$QE, digits = 2)` on 2 degrees of freedom, `r insight::format_p(by_third$QEp, stars = FALSE)`). The SCORE replication dropped the female names on the reading that the original study "did not find a difference based on the gender of the name", and the test agrees with that reading, although it shows only that this study could not detect a difference, not that none exists. The thirds show no gradient either, with the smallest gap in the middle third. The abstract of the paper speaks of a disparity "somewhat more muted in more diverse locations", a result of comparing communities by thirds of percent Black and percent Hispanic, and by types of community built from the thirds, in separate models for each group of names with population and poverty as continuous controls (pp. 20–22). The comparison by thirds on this page asks a different question, but nothing in it points that way.

## 3. Corrections with p.adjust() {#sec-corrections}

The classical answer to many tests is to make each test harder to pass. The oldest correction, named after Bonferroni, multiplies each p-value by the number of tests, so that the chance of any false rejection across the family of tests, the familywise error rate, stays at or below the chosen level. @Holm1979SimpleSequentiallyRejective gave a procedure that keeps the same guarantee and rejects more often: the p-values are sorted from the smallest, the smallest is multiplied by the number of tests, the next by one fewer, and so on, and "hypotheses are rejected one at a time until no further rejections can be done" (p. 65). @BenjaminiHochberg1995ControllingFalseDiscovery proposed controlling a different quantity, the false discovery rate, the expected share of false rejections among all rejections, and they counted among its uses the "multiple-subgroups problem, where two treatments are compared in multiple subgroups, and separate recommendations on the preferred treatments must be made for all subgroups" (p. 292). Accepting that a small share of the discoveries may be false buys more power than protecting against any false discovery at all. `p.adjust()` in base R returns the adjusted p-value of each method, which is compared with the usual 5%.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-adjusted
#| tbl-cap: "The p-values of the gap in seven subgroups, each tested on its own and adjusted for the seven tests by the methods of Holm and of Benjamini and Hochberg. The comparison of all names, the claim itself, is not part of the family. Source: `cases/housing/data/display_subgroups.csv`."
adjusted <- subgroups |>
  datawizard::data_filter(subgroup != "all names") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(holm = stats::p.adjust(p, method = "holm"),
                          bh = stats::p.adjust(p, method = "BH"))

adjusted |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", b_pp)),
                dplyr::across(c("p", "holm", "bh"), \(x) sprintf("%.4f", x))) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Subgroup = "subgroup", `Gap (points)` = "gap", p = "p",
                            Holm = "holm", `Benjamini–Hochberg` = "bh")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

Tested one at a time, `r sum(adjusted$p < 0.05)` of the seven gaps are significant at 5%. After the correction of Holm, `r sum(adjusted$holm < 0.05)` remain, the male names and the replies from other officials, and after that of Benjamini and Hochberg `r sum(adjusted$bh < 0.05)` do, with the top third of communities added. Neither correction moves an estimate, and neither changes the claim, whose comparison of all names is not part of the family. What they change is which subgroup results a reader may treat as findings in their own right, and the answer depends on the error rate chosen and on the family of tests, which here could as well have counted eight tests, or only the three thirds.

## 4. Partial pooling {#sec-pooling}

@GelmanEtAl2012WhyWeUsually argue that the problem of multiple comparisons is better met by a model than by a correction. Their abstract sets the two side by side: "Multilevel models perform partial pooling (shifting estimates toward each other), whereas classical procedures typically keep the centers of intervals stationary, adjusting for multiple comparisons by making the intervals wider." A multilevel model of subgroup effects treats the true gaps of the subgroups as varying around a common mean with a standard deviation, usually written $\tau$, that is estimated from the data. Each subgroup estimate is then pulled towards the common mean, and the more uncertain an estimate, the further it moves, so that a large gap in a small subgroup, where chance alone can produce a large departure, is discounted more than a gap estimated on many replies. Complete pooling, a single gap for all subgroups, and no pooling, a separate gap for each, are the two limits of the same model, reached when $\tau$ is zero and when it is very large.

The three thirds of communities are separate sets of replies, so the model can be fitted to their three estimates with metafor, as a random-effects model of the kind that the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-what) fits to two studies, and `blup()` returns the pooled estimate for each third.

```{r}
#| label: pooling
re_thirds <- metafor::rma(yi = b_pp, sei = se_pp, data = thirds, method = "REML")
# The ceiling of the search for the upper limit of tau is raised from its default
tau_ci <- stats::confint(re_thirds, control = list(tau2.max = 10000))$random["tau", ]
round(c(tau = sqrt(re_thirds$tau2), tau_low = tau_ci[["ci.lb"]], tau_high = tau_ci[["ci.ub"]]), 1)

# The pooled estimate of each third if the true gaps of the thirds had a
# standard deviation of 0, 5 or 10 points, or the upper limit of the interval
taus <- c(0, 5, 10, tau_ci[["ci.ub"]])
pooled <- purrr::map(taus, \(tau) {
  fit <- metafor::rma(yi = b_pp, sei = se_pp, data = thirds, tau2 = tau^2)
  tibble::tibble(third = c("lower", "middle", "top"), tau = tau, estimate = metafor::blup(fit)$pred)
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pooling
#| fig-cap: "The gap in greetings by name in the three thirds of communities by percent Hispanic, estimated separately (no pooling) and pooled by a random-effects model under four values of the standard deviation of the true gaps of the thirds, from 0 (complete pooling) to the upper limit of its 95% confidence interval. Source: `cases/housing/data/display_subgroups.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Three lines of points. Estimated separately, the lower third lies near −21, the middle near −15 and the top near −22 points. At a standard deviation of 0 all three meet at about −19; at 5 and 10 points they spread out progressively, and at the upper limit of about 24 points they lie close to the separate estimates."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| code-fold: true
dplyr::bind_rows(
  pooled |> datawizard::data_modify(model = paste0("τ = ", round(tau, 1))),
  tibble::tibble(third = c("lower", "middle", "top"), estimate = thirds$b_pp, model = "no pooling")
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(model = factor(model, levels = c(paste0("τ = ", round(taus, 1)), "no pooling"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = estimate, y = model, colour = third)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(lower = "#1d2733", middle = "#4a78ab", top = "#8b1538"),
                               name = "third of communities") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap in greetings by name, Hispanic minus white names (points)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

The model estimates $\tau$ at zero, because the three gaps differ by less than their standard errors would lead one to expect, so the estimated model pools completely and gives every third the common gap of `r insight::format_value(re_thirds$beta[[1]], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. The interval for $\tau$, however, runs from 0 to `r insight::format_value(tau_ci[["ci.ub"]], digits = 1)` points, and @fig-pooling shows why that matters: at the upper limit the pooled estimates are close to the separate ones. Three subgroups carry very little information about how much subgroups differ, and the answer of the model to the question of the third hypothesis depends on a quantity that these data can barely estimate. @GelmanEtAl2012WhyWeUsually fit their multilevel models in a Bayesian framework, in which $\tau$ receives a prior distribution and its uncertainty is carried into every pooled estimate rather than fixed at a single value, and the [Bayesian estimation module](bayesian.qmd) sets out how such a model is written in brms. The direction of the answer is nonetheless plain on this case. Corrections leave the subgroup gaps where they are and widen their intervals, while partial pooling pulls the middle third, the one subgroup whose gap looks smaller, towards the others, and with three subgroups as alike as these, most of the way.

## 5. Subgroups as forking paths {#sec-forking}

The problem of multiple comparisons is usually framed as a count of the tests that a researcher ran. @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience extend it to the tests that a researcher could have run, in what they call the 'garden of forking paths': even an analyst who runs a single test has chosen it from many that the same data allow, and if the choice was made in the light of the data, the nominal p-value no longer describes the chance of a false alarm. Subgroups are among the widest of these paths, since almost every dataset can be divided in many ways, by the sex of a name, by the person who replied, by the composition of a community or by the year of a survey, and a gap that is significant in one division can be reported as the finding while the other divisions go unmentioned.

The course handles the subgroups of this case in three ways that follow from the argument of this page. The curve of the claim leaves them out, because each subgroup asks a narrower question than the claim, so the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd#level-estimand) treats the names and the officials as decisions about the question rather than as different specifications of one question. The subgroups stay on the site as displays, all seven together, so that none of them can be read without the others. And the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-forks) decomposes the curve by its decisions, which is the same habit applied to analytical choices rather than to subgroups: every path is reported, and the spread across the paths is part of the result. A declared analysis that tests a subgroup names the subgroup, the division and the test of the difference before the data are touched, and reports whatever comes out.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Add the gap among replies within 24 hours and among later replies to the family, by filtering `ref` on `reply24` and fitting the same difference in proportions with HC2 errors, then rerun `p.adjust()` on the nine p-values and note which conclusions change. Then refit the pooling chunk to the two halves by the sex of the name instead of the three thirds, and decide whether two subgroups give the model anything to work with. Finally, write the sentence of a preregistration that would declare one subgroup analysis of this case, with its test of the difference.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The subgroup estimates are those of `display_subgroups.csv`, written by `R/housing/05_displays.R` from the course file and documented in the [codebook of the displays](../cases/housing/data/displays_codebook.md). The step-down correction is that of @Holm1979SimpleSequentiallyRejective and the false discovery rate that of @BenjaminiHochberg1995ControllingFalseDiscovery; both are implemented in `p.adjust()`, whose help page lists the other methods. The argument for partial pooling over corrections is made by @GelmanEtAl2012WhyWeUsually, the warning about differences in significance by @GelmanStern2006DifferenceSignificantNot, and the garden of forking paths is the term of @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience, while the random-effects models of section 4 are fitted with metafor [@Viechtbauer2010ConductingMetaanalysesMetafor].
